title: Gate-defined quantum dot and charge noise analysis in a Forksheet transistor
authors: Dominic Leclerc, Claude Rohrbacher, Alexis Morel, Joffrey Rivard, Romain Ritzenthaler, Christian Lupien, Hans Mertens, Naoto Horiguchi, Eva Dupont-Ferrier
abstract: We report the cryogenic characterization of a 14-nm nMOS Forksheet transistor down to 10 mK. We demonstrate that the device retains transistor operation with improved characteristics at cryogenic temperatures, while also forming a gate-defined quantum dot that can be tuned to the single-electron regime. In the quantum-dot regime, we perform low-frequency charge-noise measurements across different charge occupations and observe an average charge-noise amplitude of $\langle S_0\rangle = 10\;μ\mathrm{eV}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ at 1 Hz, with a minimum measured value of $3.3\;μ\mathrm{eV}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$. These results highlight the potential of Forksheet technology for the monolithic cointegration of quantum and classical CMOS functionalities in future quantum processors.
summary: This work reports the cryogenic characterization of a Forksheet transistor containing a gate-defined quantum dot. The authors successfully demonstrated transistor operation and observed clear Coulomb blockade features at millikelvin temperatures. Crucially, they measured the charge noise, achieving a low value comparable to state-of-the-art silicon spin qubits, highlighting the technology's potential for monolithic integration in future quantum processors.
main_problem: The study characterizes charge noise in a gate-defined quantum dot formed within a Forksheet transistor structure to assess its potential for scalable quantum computing integration.
main_result: The device retains transistor operation at cryogenic temperatures and exhibits a low average charge-noise amplitude ($\langle S_0 angle = 10 	ext{ } \mu	ext{eV}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$), comparable to state-of-the-art silicon spin-qubit devices.
method: The researchers performed cryogenic characterization, measuring transistor transfer characteristics, observing Coulomb blockade in the quantum dot regime, and quantifying charge noise via current Power Spectral Density measurements.
model_or_system: The physical system is a 14-nm nMOS Forksheet transistor fabricated on a 300 mm platform, which hosts a gate-defined quantum dot operable in the single-electron regime.
key_observables: Transistor transfer characteristics ($I_{DS}$ vs $V_G$), Coulomb blockade features, and the charge-noise amplitude $\langle S_0 angle$.
important_parameters: Cryogenic temperatures down to 10 mK; average charging energy $\langle E_C angle \approx 10 	ext{ meV}$; noise levels in the $1-10 	ext{ } \mu	ext{eV}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$ range.
main_assumptions: The noise measurement assumes the observed noise is intrinsic to the quantum dot and not dominated by setup noise or thermal fluctuations.
figures_summary: Figures show the temperature dependence of transistor characteristics (Fig. 2), stability diagrams confirming Coulomb diamonds (Fig. 3), and the charge-noise Power Spectral Density (PSD) measurements (Fig. 4).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first demonstrating basic cryogenic transistor function, then confirming quantum dot formation via Coulomb blockade, and finally quantifying the charge noise using the quantum dot as a sensitive charge sensor.
why_interesting: The demonstration of low charge noise in a standard CMOS process flow, particularly using a gate-all-around architecture, is highly relevant for developing scalable solid-state qubits and quantum processors.

Transfer characteristics of the Forksheet device as a function of temperature. a) Drain current IDS as a function of gate voltage VG at different temperatures, shown on a logarithmic scale (left axis) and a linear scale (right axis). b) Extracted subthreshold swing and threshold voltage as a function of temperature.

Example of a charge-noise measurement and comparison with other noise sources. a) Coulomb peak at VDS = 2 mV showing the three points of comparison. b) Power spectral density (PSD) measured at the three points of comparison, illustrating the range of validity of the charge-noise measurement and the Lorentzian spectral shape with a characteristic frequency f0 ∼0.1 Hz.
